Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan ------ For the petitioners 
Mr. Shah Hossain ------ For opposite party Nos. 1 and 2
parties:
Babu Miah alias A.B.M. Saidur Rahman and others ------ Petitioners
Versus
Md. Wazed Sarder and others ------ Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad, J: This Rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners calling upon the defendant-appellant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 25 of 2007 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 214 of 2000 decreeing the suit should not be set aside. 

2. The facts relevant to the disposal of the instant Rule are that on 30.1 1.2000, one Md. Nazim Uddin Miah, the father of the petitioners as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 214 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Rajbari against the opposite parties praying for declaration of title and recovery of possession in respect of 18 1/2 decimals of suit land as described in schedule "Kha" to the plaint. 
3. The facts of the plaint of the aforesaid suit, in brief, are that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Azhar Ali Miah and Mozahar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satis Chandra filed Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 in the court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that pursuant to the said compromise decree, Azhar and Mozahar were admitted as tenants and they remained in possession of the suit land as owner thereof; that Azhar Miah died leaving behind his widow Khodeja, 2 sons- Abdul Latif and Golam Sarwar and one daughter Jahanara Begum as his heirs; that the said heirs of Azhar Ali transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered sale deed being No. 4239 dated 15.06.1982 and delivered possession in his favour; that the suit land became non-cultivable as because of siltation by the flood of 1988; that the ancestral paternal residence of the defendant-opposite party No.1 was in Sujanagar, Pabna and as because of destruction of his house in Pabna by the flood in 1988, he started looking for a piece of land for residential purposes; that the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 are the distant relatives of the plaintiff and therefore, the plaintiff allowed them to live in the suit land on a temporary basis given the non-cultivable nature of .the suit land; that accordingly, the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 erected homestead in the suit land in the first part of 1989 and started living therein and planted various trees; that at that time the said defendants undertook to vacate the suit land soon after they get another piece of suitable land; that in the middle of November, 2000 they, claimed the title to the suit land on the basis of a kabuliyat from the Government and that even being requested to vacate the suit land, the said defendants refused to do so and hence, the suit. 

4. The opposite party Nos. 1-2 as defendant Nos. 1-2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that there is no cause of action to bring the present suit and the suit is not maintainable; that the suit is barred by limitation, bad for defect of parties and hit by the provisions of the Court Fees Act; that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land and as landless peasants they took lease by kabuliyat of the same from the Government on 07.12.1999 for a period of 9 years, which will expire on 28.09.2008; that they got the suit land mutated in their name and they have been enjoying and possessing the same by erecting homestead and planting trees and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

5. The defendant No.3 (the Government) also contested the suit' by filing written 
statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land has been recorded in the name of the Government as khas land and the same has been settled by leased out in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 by a registered kabuliyat and the suit land has been mutated in their name; that the plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

6. The suit was tried by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Rajbari. During trial both the parties examined 2 witnesses each of them in support of their respective cases. 

7. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Rajbari by his judgment and decree dated 29.01.2006 was pleased to decreed the suit on contest declaring that the plaintiffs have right, title and interest in the suit land and also directing the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 to remove their structures or house from the suit land and hand over the vacant possession of the same to the plaintiffs within a period of 30 days. 

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree, the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 as appellant preferred Title Appeal being No. 25 of 2007 before the learned District Judge, Rajbari. 

9. The appeal was transferred and heard by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari, who by the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 was pleased to allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. 

10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 26 of 2007, the petitioners moved this, application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 
11. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners took the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, the deposition of all the P. W.s and D. W.s and the documents exhibited by the parties and submits that the plaintiffs have lawful right, title, interest and possession in the suit land on the strength of their predecessor's registered sale deed dated 15.06.1982 (Exhibit- 5) and the said registered sale deed being a document of title, will prevail over the so-called and non-existent S.A. khatian mysteriously prepared in the name of the Government. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan placed reliance on 18 BLC (AD) 44; 13 MLR (AD) 6; 32 DLR 252; and 5 MLR 374. 

12. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan further submits that the defendants miserably failed to prove that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S. A. operation, in view of the fact that neither they adduced any minimum iota of evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention nor did they disclose the source through which or what basis or the manner in which the suit land devolved upon the Government and as such the plea of khas khatian which is the genesis of the defendants' case falls flat and therefore, the suit was rightly decreed by the trial Court. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan drew the attention to Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and referred to the decisions of Geeta Rani alais Shamima Khatun vs. Bangladesh, 36 DLR (AD) 225; Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others, 3CLR (AD) 345; and Md. Kalam Mollah and others vs. Sheikh Samsu and others, 23 BLT 320, which will be discussed later on. 

13. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan also submits that although the Government (defendant No. 3) filed a written statement and cross-examined the plaintiffs witnesses (P. W. s), 4 they did not adduce any evidence of their own in support of their contention and as such their contention as raised in their written statement having not been supported/proved by any other evidence, oral or documentary, their written statement is liable to be discarded and out of consideration. In this regard Mr. Bhuiyan refers to the decisions of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs. Hosne Ara Begum and others, 34 BLD 55; Asgar Ali Mia and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 16 BLC 37; and Sreejukta Haladhar Karmakar and others vs. Bangladesh and others 16 BLD 519. 
14. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan next submits that none of the defendants specifically denied the accuracy or genuineness of R. S. Khatian No. 259 (Exhibit- 1/Ka) and they did not take any step against the said R. S. Khatian prepared and published in the name of Satish Chandra Das and as such the same has got presumptive value of correction in view of the case, of Government of Bangladesh and others vs. Mrs. Mohsina Rahaman alias Joya as reported in 50 DLR 186 wherein it has been held that: 

"The settled law is that R.S. record has a presumption of correctness but the S.A. record has no such presumptive value." 

15. Drawing the attention to paragraph 3 of the plaint of Title Suit No.55 of 2000 (from which Civil Revision No. 2613 of 2011 arose and that Civil Revision has been heard and disposed of in simultaneous with the present Rule), Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the defendant-opposite party Nos.1 and 2 were inducted as tenants at will into the suit land on their prayer that they lost their homestead in Sujanagar, Pabna by the devastating flood of 1988, which is otherwise admitted by them in paragraph 3 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000. The relevant portion of the said paragraph is reproduced below: 

“ইং ১৯৮৮ সালের বন্যার করাল গ্রাসে বাদীর চরের বাড়ী বিনষ্ট হইলে নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি পতিত জমি হিসেবে বাদী উক্ত জমিতে ঘরবাড়ী উত্তোলন ও গাছপালা লাগাইয়া ভোগ দখলকার হয়েন ও থাকেন।”

16. On the above point as to the entry of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 into the suit land Mr. Bhuiyan submits that from the above-quoted averment as made in paragraph 3 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 it is abundantly clear that had the suit land-even been vested in the Government as khan land, the same would have been leased out by the Government in favour of any other persons and in the absence of any such lease it inevitably suggests that the suit land never devolved upon the, Government. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the entry of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 into the suit land in 1988 finding the same as vacant land is nothing but a cock and bull story in view of the fact that had the suit land been actually vacant the local people would have taken possession thereof much earlier leaving no 
room for a stranger coming from a different district called Pabna to occupy the same and erect homestead thereon. 

17. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the lower appellate court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure justice in failing to appreciate that the plaintiff-petitioners have been claiming title to 18.50 decimals of land in Plot No. 185 of R.S. Khatian No. 259 but not from R.S. Khatian No. 148 and an explanation has been offered in paragraph 3 of the plaint that  “প্রকাশ থাকে যে, বাদীর বায়ার আজাহার আলী মিয়া গংদের নিকট হইতে তাহাদের স্বত্তের কাগজপত্রের মধ্যে উক্ত খাজনার মোকদ্দমার কতক জাবেদা নকল সরবরাহ করেন ৷ উক্ত জাবেদা নকল পর্যালোচনার দেখা যায় ছোলে নামায় নালিশী আর, এস, ১৮৫ দাগটি আর.এস, ২৫৯ নং খতিয়ানের ভূমি। আর, এস, ২৫৯ নং এবং ১৪৮ নং খতিয়ানের প্রত্যেক খতিয়ানেই সতীশ চন্দ্র দাস স্বত্ববান থাকেন বিধায় বন্দোবস্ত প্রদান করেন এবং বাদীর নামীয় ইং ১৫-০৬-৮২ তারিখের 8২৩৯ নং দলিলের
গর্ভেও নালিশী আর,এস ১৮৫ নং খতিয়ানের ভূমি লিখিত হইয়াছে যাহা ভ্রমাত্মক হইতেছে৷ নালিশী আর, এস, ১৮৫ নং দাগটি বন্তুতপক্ষে আর,এস, ২৫৯ নং খতিয়াংনর ভূমি যাহা বাদীপক্ষ হইতে দাবী করতঃ ভোগ দখলকার আছেন। নালিশী জমাজমি হইতে ৫/৬ নং বিবাদী উচ্ছেদ যোগ্য হইতেছেন।”

18. On the above point Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the explanation offered in the plaint has been substantiated by evidence, and that although R. S. Khatian No. 148 instead of Khatian No. 259 (lands of both the khatians belonged to Satish Chandra Das) has been inserted in the sale deed dated 15.06.1982, the same has in no way affected the right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiff-petitioners in the suit land since they had been enjoying and possessing the same openly, adversely and peacefully to the knowledge of all concerned including the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 since their predecessor's sale deed dated 15.06.1982 and no one raised any objection claiming title to the suit land. 

19. Taking to paragraph 7 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 whereto the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 are the plaintiffs, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that their suit is premature in view of the fact that their so-called kabuliyat was not cancelled, rather the same was merely threatened to be cancelled and such threat of cancellation as opposed to any final decision actually cancelling the lease is not a cause of action and therefore, the said suit being based on a mere apprehension, is without any cause of action and liable to be dismissed. In this regard Mr. Bhuiyan placed reliance on paragraph 7 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 is reproduced below: 

“৭। সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি), রাজবাড়ী সদর নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি সংক্রান্তে ইং ১২/০৩/২০০০ তাং স্বাক্ষরিত নোটিশ বাদী প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ইং ৩/৪/২০০০ তাং সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি), রাজবাড়ী সদর নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি সংক্রান্তে কবুলিয়াত বাতিলের জন্য হুমকি প্রদর্শন করায় অত্র নালিশের কারণ উদ্ভব হইয়াছে।”

20. Mr. Bhuiyan continues to submit that the lower appellate court failed to appreciate that the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents was totally in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner and against the opposite. parties and that the petitioner has been able to prove his lawful right, title, interest and possession in and dispossession from the suit land by both documentary and oral evidence through competent witnesses of convincing nature and as such the court of appeal below ought to have dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. 

21. Mr. Bhuiyan lastly submits that the trial court correctly decreed the suit on merit upon proper assessment of the pleadings, evidence and other Materials on record, but the court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision since as the final court of fact, did not apply its judicial mind and independently assess the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, rather turned down the decision of the trial court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial court and as, such the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside, and in support of his submission Mr. Bhuiyan has placed reliance on the decisions reported in XII ADC 751; 14 BLD 229; 17 BLD 47; 10MLR 255; 15 BLD 96. 

22. On the other hand, Mr. Shah Hossain the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 submits that on and from 14th April, 1956 the rent receiving interest of all the rent receivers in Bangladesh having been acquired by the Government under Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT Act), the plaintiff-petitioners claim of title to the suit land on the strength of a compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 drawn up in Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 between the then Zaminder/landlord Satish Chandra Das and his tenants Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah from whom the petitioners got the suit land by way of successive transfers becomes barred by law. In support of his submission, Mr. Hossain referred to the decisions reported in 31 DLR (AD) 323; 14 BLC 848; 38 DLR (AD) 93; and 20 DLR 699. Amongst the cited decisions, I feel the necessity to quote the ratio decidendi of the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh vs. Abani Kanta Chakraborty and others 38 DLR (AD) 93, which runs as follows: 

"After the abolition of all rent receiving interests in the country there is only one class of tenancy under the Government whose rights and liabilities are governed by an uniform law." 

23. Controverting the above submission readily, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit having been filed within 3 (three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period before Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 and therefore, the compromise decree drawn up in that suit is legal, whereby the landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired title to the suit land by a registered sale deed 16.07.2000 are the lawful title 
holders of the suit land. 
24. Mr. Shah Hossain also submits that the plaintiff-petitioners produced and exhibited the certified copy of their title deed in support of their claim to the suit land without any formal proof thereof and as such those secondary evidence in support of their title is not admissible in law within the meaning of Section 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act, 1872. To substantiate his submission, Mr. Hossain cited the decisions reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45; 41 DLR (AD) 97 and 14 BLC (AD) 132. In the case of Soya Rani Guha alias Soya Rani Gupta vs. Abdul Awal Miah and others 47 DLR (AD) 45 it has been held that: 

"A party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even where a document is exhibited without objection the Court is to be satisfied as to its execution. " 

25. In reply to the above submission, Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan submits that the certified copy of the title deed of the plaintiff-petitioners is admissible in law within the meaning of Section 79 of the Evidence Act, 1872, in view of the fact that as a registered document that sale deed carries the presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein and if the opposite parties intend to dispute that presumption they are required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement (Shishir Kanti Pal and others vs. Nur Mohammad and others 55 DLR (AD) 39). In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the decision reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39 being later in point of time will prevail over the one reported 47 DLR (AD) 45.

26. Mr. Shah Hossain next submits that the S. A. Khatian prepared and published in the name of the Government vis-a-vis the suit land shall be presumed to be correct unless and until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. In this connection Mr. Hossain referred to Section 19(3) and 144A of the SAT Act and the decisions reported in 9 MLR (AD) 82; 30 DLR (SC) 81; 6 BLC 241; 33 DLR 126; 17 BLC (AD) 174; and 61 DLR 18. 

27. Mr. Shah Hossain finally submits that the trial Court wrongly shifted the burden of proving the correctness of S. A. Khatian on the defendant-opposite parties and held that the defendants failed to proves as to how, why and when the suit land became the khas land of the Government by adducing any evidence, oral and documentary. On this point Mr. Hossain further submits that as plaintiff-the petitioners ought to have proved their case, they cannot take the advantage of the weakness of the defendants. Supporting the impugned judgment and decree Mr. Hossain lastly submits that the appellate court below as the final court of fact arrived at a proper decision upon proper assessment of the pleadings of the parties, evidence and other materials on record and as such the same does not call for any interference from this Court. 

28. I have meticulously gone through the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, evidence led by them and other materials on record and also heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the decisions relied upon by both the parties with utmost circumspection and the relevant provisions of law wherefrom it transpires that the evidentiary value of the registered sale deed of the plaintiff-petitioners (Exhibit- 5), the preparation and publication of S. A. record of rights, if any, in the khas khatian of the Government as well as the maintainability of Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 are predominant issues in this case apart from other connected issues and I will endeavour to address all the issues in proportion to their respective weight and importance. 

29. It appears from the certified copy of the sale deed dated 15.06.1982 that the plaintiffs acquired title to the suit land on the strength of the same and the said registered sale deed being a document of title, will prevail over the so-called and non-existent S. A. khatian mysteriously prepared in the name of the Government as our Appellate Division has correctly held in the case of Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan and others vs. Md. Nasir Hossain and others, 18 BLC (AD) 44 in the following language: 

"Registered document prevail upon record of right- SA and RS records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and that the registered document would remain in force unless the same was cancelled by an appropriate civil court." 

30. It is the case of the defendant-opposite parties that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S. A. operation, but none of them adduced any evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention. Again, although the Government filed a written statement, they did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, to show as to when, why and how the suit land became khas in their name and as such the written statement of the Government will not ipso facto be admissible in evidence unless and until the same is supported by competent witnesses of convincing nature, and as such Section 92 of the SAT Act as well as the decisions referred to by the plaintiff-petitioner will stand in the way of the claim of defendants. At this juncture I think it is necessary to quote Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, which runs as follows: 
92. (1) The interest of a raiyat in a holding shall he extinguished 
(a) when he dies intestate leaving no heir entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject; 
(b) when he surrenders his holding at the end of any agricultural year by giving notice in the prescribed form and in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period to the Revenue-officer; 
(c) when he voluntarily abandons his residence without making any arrangement for payment of the rent as it falls due and cesses to cultivate his holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of; servants or labourers or with the aid of partners cr bargadars for a period of three successive years; or 
(d) when such interest has devolved by inheritance, under the law of inheritance to which such raiyat is subject, on a person who is not a bona fide cultivator and such person has not cultivated the land comprised in the holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargadars during the period of five years from the date on which such interest has so devolved on him and there is no sufficient cause why he has not so cultivated the land. 

(2) When the interest of a raiyat in a holding is extinguished under sub-section (1), the Revenue-officer may enter on the holding; and the holding shall, with effect from the date on which the Revenue-officer so enters on it, vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances except the encumbrances on the holding which is extinguished under clause (a) of the said sub-section, but the persons whose interests in the holdings are extinguished under clauses (b), (c) and (d) of that sub-section shall continue to be personally liable for the money secured by the encumbrances on such holdings. 
(3) Before entering on a holding under sub-section (2), the Revenue-officer shall cause a notice to be published in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to so enter on the holding and specifying the reasons thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objections that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the notice and shall record a decision. 

In the case of Bangladesh and others vs. Mall ick Ali Ahmed and others, 3CLR (AD) 345 it has been held that: 

"The treating of the suit land as escheat property by the government and thereby declaring the same as khas land of the government without making it clear in any manner as to how and why the suit property can be treated as escheat property- has been illegal. " 

31. It is pertinent to mention here that the Government although remained silent and did not turn up either before the Courts below or before this Court in the course of the Rule hearing to establish its claim to the suit land and therefore, the defendants signally failed to prove that the suit land ever vested in the Government as khas land, in view of the Government's failure to adduce evidence in support of its written statement. This view finds support from the case of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs. Hosne Ara Begum and others 34 BLD 55 wherein it has been held that: 

"The filing of the written statement without giving any oral testimony in support of the same before the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not he considered ipso facto as evidence, rather, either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence." 

32. It appears from Ext. 2 that Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das against his tenants Mozahar Ali Miah and Azahar Ali Miah for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit was filed within 3 (three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force as on 14'n April, 1956 and hence, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 , and therefore, the compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 (Ext. 2) drawn up in that Rent Suit is also legal. In this connection Court think it would be profitable to quote Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, which runs as follows: 

Description of suit	Period of limitation	Time from which period begins to run
110. For arrears of rent.	Part VI- Three years (cntd) Three years	When the arrears become due 


33. It also appears from the abovementioned compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 that landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali as his tenants for the period before Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioner having acquired title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 2 (three) separate registered sale deeds dated 01.03.1961 (Ext. 2 of Title Suit No. 154 of 2000) and 15.06.2000 (Ext. 5) from them and their transferees, arc the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

34. It is a settled principle of law that the plaintiff has to proves his case on the balance of probabilities and he/she cannot bank or capitalize on the weakness of the defendant. It is also a settled proposition that burden of proof shifts and the question of onus loses importance when both the sides adduce evidence in support of their claim and defence. In the case of Muhammad Ishaque vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury and others II ADC 50 our apex Court held that ".... It is well-settled that when both the parties have led evidence question of onus is out of place and the matter is to be decided on the evidence led by the parties. " 

35. In the panorama as canvassed in the foregoing paragraph, it can be safely concluded that the defendants are not absolved of their obligation to prove as to when, why and how the suit land was recorded in the khas khatian of the Government and that obligation having not been discharged by any of the defendants, the plea of khas khatian is not proved at all. Moreover, it has already been held in Civil Revision No. 2613 of 2011 arising out of Title Suit No. 55 of 200 to which the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are plaintiffs that the opposite parties of the present Rule signally failed to prove their plea as to khas khatian. 

36. It appears from R. S. Khatian No. 259 (Ext. 1/Ka) that R. S. Plot No. 185 is present in the said khatian showing 37 decimals of land in sixteen annas share and on scrutiny of R. S. Khatian No. 148, it is found that Plot No. 285 appears therein, but the quantum of land in the said plot is completely different, namely 15 decimals in eight annas share, and thus, I am of the view that the explanation offered in the plaint as to the insertion of R. S. Khatian No. 148 in lieu of R. S. Khatian it No. 259 in the compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 as drawn up in Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 and the subsequent sale deeds appears to be plausible and acceptable. 

37. It appears from paragraph 3 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 that the 
opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 entered into the suit land after the flood of 1988, whereas they allegedly took settlement of the same in 1999 and they did not at all clarify in their pleadings submitted and evidence adduced in all the suits in what capacity they possessed and enjoyed the suit land for the intervening period between 1988 and 1999 and as such I am constrained to hold the view that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land as mere trespassers. Moreover, Court think that if the suit land had ever been recorded in the khas khatian of the Government, it would have settled the same in favour of anyone else, and in the absence of any such lease, Government's title as well as the interest of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in the suit land is not proved at all. 

38. Furthermore, the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs stated in paragraph 7 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari (defendant No. 4 to the said suit) by his letter dated 12.03.2000 merely threatened to cancel his kabuliyat, but at no point of time his lease was actually cancelled, and the threat of cancellation as opposed to any actual cancellation cannot be cause of his grievance and therefore, Title Suit No. 55 of 2000 filed by the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 was held to be premature and liable to be dismissed as being not maintainable in law as per the decision given in the case of Kamaluddin (Md.) and another vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, Bangladesh and others 56 DLR (AD) 212 wherein it has been held that: 
"Unless final order is passed in a matter, person interested in the matter or persons apprehensive of being affected by the act of the functionaries performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority is not entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction." 

39. It is worth to mention here that although the above decision has been made in a writ petition, the same extends to civil jurisdiction as well given the fact that writ jurisdiction forms part of civil jurisdiction. 

40. As I have already found that the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 are mere trespassers into the suit land, they have got no locus standi to question the accuracy or genuineness of the title deed of the plaintiff petitioners however defective title the latter might have to the suit land. On the 'balance of probabilities' which is the standard of proof in civil jurisdiction as opposed to 'beyond reasonable double' in criminal jurisdiction and also on the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents available in the records of the suit, it appears to me that the plaintiff-petitioners have lawful title to the suit land, which can be questioned only by a person having a better title thereto. That being so, the suit of the plaintiffs succeeds and the defendants having failed to prove their better title to the suit land than that of the plaintiffs, they are entitled to a decree as prayed for. 

41. On perusal of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, I am of the considered view that the judgment of the trial court is very much sound, proper and in accordance with law for, the reasons stated above and it does not suffer from any misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the suit and as such I. find no reason to interfere with the same. On the other hand, the court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision by failing to apply its judicial mind to the given set of facts and failed to independently assess the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and turned down to the decision of the trial court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial court and as such the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside. 

42. Accordingly, this Court finds merit in the Rule for which it In the result the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 25 of 2007 allowing the appeal is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 214 of 2000 decreeing the suit is hereby affirmed. 

43. No order as to cost. 

44. Send down the lower Court record along with a copy of this judgment to the Court concerned, at once.

End.
